nodes.name: Loss function
nodes.statement: A loss function L(w) maps the parameters w to one number that measures how badly the model fits the data. Training means finding a w that makes L small.

nodes.name: Linear approximation
nodes.statement: Near a point w, the loss is close to its tangent plane, L(w + d) ≈ L(w) + ∇L(w)·d for a small step d.

nodes.name: Gradient points uphill
nodes.statement: The gradient ∇L(w) points in the direction in which L increases fastest. Its length is the rate of that increase.

nodes.name: Negative gradient descends
nodes.statement: A small step d = −α∇L(w) lowers the loss whenever ∇L(w) ≠ 0, because the linear term becomes −α‖∇L(w)‖², which is negative.

nodes.name: Learning rate
nodes.statement: The learning rate α > 0 sets how far each step moves along the negative gradient.

nodes.name: GD update step
nodes.statement: Gradient descent repeats the update w ← w − α∇L(w) until the loss stops improving.

nodes.name: Stationary points are fixed
nodes.statement: The update leaves w unchanged exactly when ∇L(w) = 0. So gradient descent can only come to rest at a stationary point.

nodes.name: Convex loss
nodes.statement: A function is convex when the straight segment between any two points of its graph lies on or above the graph. For a twice differentiable loss, this holds exactly when every Hessian eigenvalue is ≥ 0.

nodes.name: Local minima are global
nodes.statement: For a convex loss, every stationary point is a global minimum. So gradient descent on a convex loss cannot get stuck in a worse local minimum.

nodes.name: Hessian curvature
nodes.statement: The Hessian H is the symmetric matrix of second derivatives of L. Its eigenvalues λ give the curvature of the loss along its eigenvectors.

nodes.name: Quadratic model
nodes.statement: Near a minimum w*, where the gradient is zero, the loss is well approximated by L(w) ≈ L(w*) + ½(w − w*)ᵀH(w − w*).

nodes.name: Error update on a quadratic
nodes.statement: On the quadratic model the gradient is H(w − w*). So the error e = w − w* follows e ← (I − αH)e at every step.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue decoupling
nodes.statement: Writing the error in the eigenvectors of H splits the update into independent coordinates. Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, each step multiplies the error by (1 − αλ).

nodes.name: Convergence condition
nodes.statement: The error shrinks along every eigendirection if and only if |1 − αλ| < 1 for every λ. For positive eigenvalues this means 0 < α < 2/λ_max.

nodes.name: Overshoot past minimum
nodes.statement: When 1/λ < α < 2/λ, the factor 1 − αλ is negative, so the error flips sign each step while still shrinking. When α > 2/λ, the flips grow and the iterates diverge.

nodes.name: Condition number κ
nodes.statement: The condition number κ = λ_max/λ_min measures how stretched the loss bowl is. A round bowl has κ = 1, and a long narrow valley has a large κ.

nodes.name: Zigzag in valleys
nodes.statement: In a long narrow valley, a step size that makes progress along the flat direction overshoots in the steep direction. The iterates bounce from wall to wall while creeping slowly along the valley floor.

nodes.name: Rate 1 − 1/κ
nodes.statement: With α = 1/λ_max, the flattest direction shrinks by a factor of 1 − λ_min/λ_max = 1 − 1/κ per step. So the number of steps to reach a fixed accuracy grows roughly in proportion to κ.

nodes.name: Lipschitz smoothness
nodes.statement: A loss is β-smooth when ‖∇L(u) − ∇L(v)‖ ≤ β‖u − v‖ for all u and v. For a twice differentiable loss, this means no Hessian eigenvalue is larger than β in size.

nodes.name: Descent lemma
nodes.statement: For a β-smooth loss, one gradient step with α = 1/β lowers the loss by at least ‖∇L(w)‖²/(2β).

nodes.name: Safe step size
nodes.statement: Any step size 0 < α < 2/β makes each gradient step decrease a β-smooth loss. This bound needs only β, not the exact eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Loss as an average
nodes.statement: The training loss is an average over n examples, L(w) = (1/n) Σ ℓᵢ(w), so its gradient is the average of the per-example gradients. Computing it exactly costs one pass over all n examples.

nodes.name: Unbiased stochastic gradient
nodes.statement: If one example i is picked uniformly at random, the expectation of its gradient ∇ℓᵢ(w) equals the full gradient ∇L(w). So a stochastic step points downhill on average.

nodes.name: SGD update
nodes.statement: Stochastic gradient descent replaces ∇L(w) in the update with the gradient of one random example or a small random batch. Each step then costs a tiny fraction of a full pass.

nodes.name: Variance shrinks with batch size
nodes.statement: Averaging the gradients of B independently sampled examples divides the variance of the estimate by B. Its standard deviation, the typical size of the noise, shrinks like 1/√B.

nodes.name: SGD noise floor
nodes.statement: With a constant learning rate, SGD keeps jittering in a region around the minimum whose size grows with α and with the gradient variance. Shrinking α over time lets the iterates settle.

nodes.name: Momentum update
nodes.statement: Momentum keeps a velocity v ← μv − α∇L(w) and moves w ← w + v, with μ between 0 and 1. Gradients that keep pointing the same way add up, and gradients that flip sign cancel.

nodes.name: Momentum damps zigzag
nodes.statement: In a narrow valley, momentum cancels the alternating steps across the steep direction. It builds up speed along the flat direction, where the gradient keeps the same sign.

nodes.name: √κ speedup
nodes.statement: On a quadratic with well-tuned α and μ, momentum shrinks the error by a factor near 1 − 2/√κ per step. Plain gradient descent manages only about 1 − 1/κ, so momentum needs roughly √κ times fewer steps.
